You master at B2 level the fine differences between ser and estar: adjectives that change meaning (ser listo / estar listo, ser rico / estar rico, ser verde / estar verde, ser malo / estar malo, ser aburrido / estar aburrido), "estar de" (de vacaciones, de pie, de camarero), "ser" for where an event takes place (la boda es en Triana) and the passive with ser versus the result with estar (fue publicado / está publicado).
The truck is already ready to leave.
Álex is very clever, but today he's tired.
The presentation takes place at the library.
To use adjectives that change meaning with ser and estar: listo, rico, verde, malo, bueno, aburrido, vivo, despierto, atento.
To use "estar de" for temporary situations: de vacaciones, de viaje, de pie, de buen humor, de camarero.
To use "ser" for the place and time of an event: la fiesta es en casa de Ana, el examen es a las nueve.
To distinguish the passive with ser (the action) from estar + participle (the result): la carta fue escrita / la carta está escrita.
To avoid typical mistakes made by Romanians: "soy casado" versus "estoy casado", "es muerto" versus "está muerto".
Thursday, 14 January, evening, in Costel's daughter's flat in Valencia. Costel has just arrived after four days on the road. Irina, his daughter, has made paella. Álex is fifteen.
Dad, you're very thin. Have you eaten anything in four days?
Sandwiches. But this paella is delicious. Did you make it?
She made it, but the recipe is the neighbour's, and she's from Alzira.
Dad, you speak perfect Spanish. I'm… I don't know. I'm very proud.
It isn't perfect. But I'm no longer lost when people talk.
Grandpa, are you ready for tomorrow? We have to be at school at eight.
I'm ready. The walnuts are in the cab. Where is the planting?
In the school garden, behind the gym. The biology teacher is delighted.
And I'm on holiday tomorrow. I've taken the day off.
Then tomorrow there are three of us. Like when Álex was little.
"estar de vacaciones" = to be on holiday
The superlative in -ísimo is always stressed on "í": ri-QUÍ-si-mo, lis-TÍ-si-mo, bue-NÍ-si-mo. "qui" is read "kee".
"c" before "e, i" is pronounced in Spain like English "th", and "z" the same: Va-LEN-thia, Al-THI-ra. In southern Spain and in Latin America you hear "s".
Single "r" between vowels (fron-TE-ra), rolled "r" after "n" (fron-): the tongue taps several times.
green in colour: El letrero es verde.
unripe / not ready: La naranja está verde.
ill / gone off: Está malo; la leche está mala.
sharp, lively: Es un niño muy vivo.
attentive: Está atento a la carretera.
General rule: ser = what someone or something is (identity, character); estar = how it is now (state, result). With the adjectives in the table, the difference becomes a difference in meaning.
During the ceremony everyone was standing.
This summer Curro is working (temporarily) as a waiter in a bar in Triana.
Today the teacher is in a good mood.
"Es camarero" = it's his profession. "Está de camarero" = he is working as a waiter temporarily, but it isn't his main job.
3. Where and when it takes place: ser
an object, a person, a place
Las nueces están en la cabina.
La plantación es en el huerto escolar.
La función es a las cinco.
La receta es de la vecina; la vecina es de Alzira.
Typical mistake: "La boda está en Triana". Correct: «La boda es en Triana» (event), but «Los novios están en Triana» (people).
La carta está escrita a mano.
Faustino está casado. El abuelo Vasile está muerto.
In Romanian we say "e căsătorit", "e mort" with the same verb. In Spanish, both take "estar": «está casado», «está muerto». "Ser casado" isn't used in Spain.
"The concert takes place in the square."
El concierto es en la plaza.
El concierto está en la plaza.
El concierto hay en la plaza.
¿Qué le dice Irina a su padre al principio?
¿De quién es la receta de la paella?
Costel writes to Ecaterina, on a postcard, from the viewpoint where you first see the sea. Notice ser and estar.
Dear doña Ecaterina: I'm at the viewpoint. Don Andrés's stretch is narrow and full of bends, but it's the same as in the atlas.
The sea is grey today, because it's cloudy. But it's the same sea. That seems to me the most important thing.
There is a stone bench that is very old. You probably sat here. I sat for five minutes, for both of you. Costel.
¿Cómo está el tramo de don Andrés?
¿Cuánto tiempo se sienta Costel en el banco?

On Monday, 11 January, at a quarter to five in the morning, the haulage company's car park was dark and frozen. Costel had been there since four, checking for the fourth time the tyres, the lights and the load: twenty-two tonnes of furniture for a warehouse in Requena, a town in the interior of the province of Valencia. The truck was ready. So was he, more or less. At ten to five two cars appeared. Out of the first got Mr Dan, in a woollen hat, with the steel flask in his hand, full of coffee. Out of the second got Ana and Ecaterina, who had insisted on coming to see him off even though it was five in the morning and twelve degrees below zero.

Ecaterina gave him a sealed envelope. She told him not to open it until he was in front of the sea, at the viewpoint on don Andrés's stretch, and that if he didn't find the viewpoint, he should never open it. Costel put it in his jacket pocket, next to Rosa Elena's drawing, which he had carried there since the B2 exam. Mr Dan gave him the flask and a laminated sheet: the table of rest areas, with the exact time of each stop. Ana hugged him and gave him a bag of food Carmen had prepared the night before, because, according to Carmen, on Europe's motorways the food was expensive and bad, and a hungry trucker was a public danger.

At five on the dot, Costel set off. The three of them stayed in the car park, watching the truck's red lights move away along the ring road until they disappeared. Nobody said anything for a while. Then Mr Dan looked at his watch and said that, if everything went according to the table, Costel would be at the Hungarian border at half past eleven. Ana told him he wouldn't be calm until Thursday. Mr Dan denied it. He said he was perfectly calm, and that he had noted the time of every stop on his phone purely for technical reasons. Ecaterina laughed for the first time that morning, her nose red with cold.

The first day was long and boring, as first days on the road always are. Romania, the border, the whole of Hungary under a thick fog that didn't let you see anything beyond fifty metres. Costel slept in a service area near Budapest, in the bunk in the cab, with his hat on. Before falling asleep he called Mr Dan, as he had promised, and told him he was fine, tired but happy, and that the coffee in the flask was still hot after fourteen hours. Mr Dan told him that was thermodynamically impossible. Costel replied that, in that case, the flask was a better engineer than he was.

On the second day he crossed Slovenia and northern Italy. In a service area near Verona, while he was having a coffee at the bar, an Italian trucker of about forty asked him something in Italian. Costel didn't understand all of it, but answered in Spanish, just to try. The Italian understood perfectly and answered in Italian, slowly. They talked for half an hour, each in his own language, about trucks, children and how bad the food on the motorways was. When they said goodbye, the Italian asked him if he was Spanish. Costel told him no, that he was Romanian, but that he was learning. The Italian told him that, in that case, he was learning very well.

On the third day he crossed France along the coast, between Nice and Montpellier, with the sea on his left for hours, blue and calm. But Costel didn't look at it much. He had promised Ecaterina that the first real sea of that trip would be the one at don Andrés's viewpoint, and a trucker keeps his promises, even if they are a little absurd. Towards evening he reached the Pyrenees, at La Jonquera. There was no snow. It was cloudy, and a cold wind was blowing that shook the truck as if it were made of paper. When he passed the blue sign that said "España", Costel honked twice, although there was nobody to hear it.

That night he slept in a service area near Girona. It was the first time in his life that he spoke Spanish in Spain with someone who didn't know him. It was with the waitress at the bar, an older woman with a Catalan accent, who asked him what he wanted for dinner. Costel ordered a potato tortilla and a glass of red wine. The waitress asked him where he was from. Costel told her he was from Romania, that he was passing through, and that he was going to Valencia to see his daughter and grandson. The waitress told him he spoke very well. Costel thanked her and told her he had learned in his truck cab. The waitress didn't charge him for the wine.

On the fourth day, Thursday the 14th, Costel drove down the Mediterranean motorway to Valencia and carried on inland, to Requena, where the warehouse was. He unloaded the furniture at midday. The warehouse manager, a fat, friendly man called Vicente, signed his papers and asked him if it was his first time there. Costel said yes. Vicente asked him if he needed anything. Costel showed him the 1980 atlas, open at the page with the pencil line, and asked him if the old road still existed. Vicente put on his glasses, looked at the atlas for a long time and told him yes, it existed, but hardly anyone used it any more.

He explained that it was a narrow road, full of bends, that went down from the plateau towards the coast between mountains, and that it could be done with an empty truck, though you had to go very slowly. He asked him why he was interested. Costel told him, in five minutes, the story of don Andrés, Ecaterina and the trip of July 1979. Vicente took off his glasses. He was silent for a moment. Then he told him that his father had also driven down that road many times, with a truck full of oranges, in the seventies, and that he had gone with him as a boy, sitting in the cab. He told him that halfway down there was a viewpoint. And that from there you saw the sea for the first time.

Costel took the old road at three in the afternoon, with the empty truck. It was exactly as Vicente had described it: narrow, with tight bends, with small villages of white houses and leafless almond trees on the slopes. In the twenty-three kilometres Mr Dan had marked with a red flag, he didn't pass a single other car. He drove very slowly, in second gear, with the windows down despite the cold, because he wanted to smell the air. He thought that in July 1979 that air must have smelled of pine and heat. In January it smelled of wet earth and firewood. And, at the end of a bend, without warning, the viewpoint appeared.

It was a small patch of open ground, with a low stone wall and an old bench, also of stone. Below, very far away, between the mountains, you could see the plain of orange groves and, at the end, a grey strip that merged with the sky: the sea. That day it wasn't blue, because it was cloudy. But it was the sea. Costel parked the truck, got out and sat on the bench. He stayed there a while doing nothing, looking. Then he took Ecaterina's envelope out of his pocket and opened it. Inside was a small black-and-white photo with white edges. It was that very bench. And on the bench, two young people sitting, laughing, with the sea behind them.

On the back of the photo, in Ecaterina's handwriting, there was a sentence: "July 1979. Taken by a man passing by, with our camera. Andrés thanked him in three languages. Sit for a moment for us." Costel looked at the photo for a long time. Andrés had black hair and a white shirt. Ecaterina was wearing a flowered dress and had long hair, and she was laughing with her mouth open, like Rosa Elena. He was looking at her, not at the camera. Costel thought it was the photo of two people who didn't yet know they would be separated for forty years. And he thought that perhaps it was better that way, that they didn't know.

He sat on the bench for five minutes, for both of them, as Ecaterina had asked. Then he took a photo of the empty bench with his phone, with the grey sea in the background, from the same angle as the 1979 photo. He sent it to Ecaterina with a short message: "I'm at the viewpoint. The bench is the same. The sea is grey, but it's the same." Ecaterina replied a minute later. She was in Bucharest, on the balcony, at four in the afternoon, with the little lamp lit although it was still daylight. She wrote a single word: "Thank you." And underneath, another sentence: "Now you can look at the sea as much as you like."

Costel arrived at his daughter's at half past six, after leaving the truck in a truck park at the port. Irina lived in a neighbourhood near the sea, in a seventh-floor flat with a balcony so small that not even a chair fitted on it, as Álex had said. When she opened the door, she stood looking at her father without saying anything. She hadn't seen him in person for almost two years. She told him he was very thin. Costel told her she was the same as always, which was a lie, because she was prettier. Álex appeared behind his mother. He was taller than Costel. Costel hadn't expected that. He shook his hand, like a man's, and then hugged him, like a child.

They had paella for dinner, which Irina had made with the recipe of the neighbour on the fourth floor, who was from Alzira and said that real paella was only made in Valencia and only on Sundays, but that for a grandfather coming from Romania by truck an exception could be made. Costel said it was delicious. Irina told him he spoke perfect Spanish and burst into tears. Costel told her it wasn't perfect, but that he was no longer lost when people talked. Álex said nothing for a while. Then he asked his grandfather, in Spanish, whether he was ready for the next day, because they had to be at school at eight, for the planting.

The planting was on Friday, 15 January, at half past eight, in the school garden of Álex's secondary school, behind the gym. Present were Álex; Irina, who had taken the day off; Costel; the biology teacher, who was delighted with the idea; and Álex's whole class, twenty-five half-asleep teenagers with their hands in their pockets. The teacher explained to them that a walnut tree took about ten years to produce walnuts, and that it lived for more than a hundred. That this tree, therefore, would belong to all the pupils who passed through the school for a century. Then she asked Costel to tell them where those walnuts came from. Costel got very nervous. But he told them.

He told them they came from a walnut tree in a village in the Carpathians, almost a hundred years old, like its owner. That the owner was called Gheorghe, that he had learned to read at thirty in the army, and that every evening he lit an oil lamp at seven. That this walnut tree had seen weddings, birthdays, snowfalls and a C1 exam recounted on the porch. And that Grandpa Gheorghe had told him orange trees bore fruit in three years, but walnut trees in ten, and that was why you had to start early. The teenagers were no longer asleep. A girl in the front row asked him if Grandpa Gheorghe was alive. Costel told her yes, very much alive.

Álex dug the hole with a spade taller than he was. Costel gave him a walnut from the bag, the biggest one, and Álex buried it five centimetres deep, as the teacher had explained. They planted two more beside it, just in case, in case the first one didn't germinate. The teacher told them she would put up a sign. Álex suggested what it should say. The sign, which the art teacher painted that same afternoon in green letters, was hanging from a stake the following Monday: "Gheorghe's walnut tree. Planted on 15 January. So that our grandchildren can see it." Irina took a photo of the sign and sent it to everyone.

15 January was also Rosa Elena's birthday. She was turning six. That afternoon, in Bucharest, at Ana and Mihai's, there was a party with fourteen children from the Spanish club, a cake in the shape of a camera made by Mrs Florica, and a video call at six, Bucharest time, with Valencia. Costel and Álex sang "Cumpleaños feliz" to her in Spanish from Irina's tiny balcony, squashed like sardines. Then Álex showed her the photo of the walnut tree's sign. Rosa Elena looked at it very seriously and said it was the best birthday present she had ever been given, even though it wasn't for her. Then she asked them to send her a walnut.

Costel spent the weekend in Valencia. On Saturday morning he went to the beach with Álex, although it was windy and the sea was grey and rough. They took off their shoes and put their feet in the water, which was icy. Álex asked him why he had wanted to learn Spanish, at his age. Costel thought about the answer for a while. He told him that at first it had been for him, so that he could talk to him when he spoke Spanish with his mother and he didn't understand a thing. That then it had been for the exams. And that now it was for something he couldn't explain, something to do with sitting on a stone bench for two people you never met.

On Monday the 18th, at dawn, he loaded the truck with twenty-four tonnes of oranges at a warehouse in Alzira, the hometown of Irina's neighbour. The oranges were perfect, neither unripe nor overripe, and they smelled so strongly that the whole cab smelled of oranges. The warehouse manager gave him a separate crate, of the best ones, for his family. Costel set off for Romania at six in the morning. Irina and Álex saw him off at the port car park, as Mr Dan, Ana and Ecaterina had seen him off in Bucharest a week earlier. Álex told him he would expect him in two weeks. Costel told him he would be there. And to remember to water the walnut tree.

Meanwhile, in Bucharest, Ecaterina had kept her promise to visit the Spanish club. It was on Friday the 22nd, at four. Rosa Elena introduced her with a speech that, after many negotiations with Mrs Ionescu, had come down from twenty-two minutes to three. She said that Ecaterina was a translator, that she had translated García Márquez, that she had written a book in Spanish about a lamp and that she was her grandmother, although not really. Then she gave her the floor. The children asked her questions for an hour. Tudor asked her if she was famous. Ecaterina answered that she wasn't famous, but that day she was very happy, and that was much better.

A very little girl in the back row asked her what was the hardest thing to translate. Ecaterina thought for a moment. She told her the hardest thing was the verbs "ser" and "estar", because in Romanian there was only one. She explained that in Spanish "ser aburrido" wasn't the same as "estar aburrido", nor "ser listo" the same as "estar listo", and that once, when she was young, she had translated "el niño está malo" as "the child is wicked", and the poor child in the novel had been wicked in Romanian for thirty years, until someone noticed in the second edition. The children laughed a lot. Mrs Ionescu, at the back, wrote it all down in her notebook.

In Madrid, that same week, "La librera de Triana" went to press. Marta sent Faustino the final proofs, so that he could read them before anyone else, and Faustino did something he hadn't told anyone about: for five evenings in a row, at seven, instead of opening a book at random in the bookshop doorway, he read a chapter of the novel aloud. The neighbours in Triana sat on the kerb to listen to him. Doña Remedios listened from inside, behind the counter, without coming out, because she said it was very strange to be a listener in your own story. On the fifth day, when Faustino read the wedding chapter, the neighbours applauded.

Costel got back to Bucharest on Thursday the 21st in the evening, with the oranges. The next day, before returning the truck, he made a round that wasn't in any of Mr Dan's tables. He left a bag of oranges at Ana and Mihai's, another at Ecaterina's, another at Mr Dan's and another at Mrs Florica's. And on Saturday he went to the village, with the crate of the best ones, for Grandpa Gheorghe. He showed him the photo of the Valencia walnut tree's sign on his phone. Grandpa asked him to read it to him twice. Then he was silent for a long time, peeling an orange with his penknife, very slowly, in a single long strip, as he used to do when he was young.

When he had finished, he gave half the orange to Costel and told him just one thing: that now he had a walnut tree in Spain, and that meant he was no longer just an old man from a village in the Carpathians, but an old man from two places. Costel asked him whether that was good. Grandpa told him it was the best thing that had happened to him since he learned to read. Then he asked him, on the next trip, to take a photo of the walnut tree every time, even if it hadn't come up out of the ground yet, so he could see how it grew. Costel promised he would. Grandpa told him that, in that case, he had to live at least ten more years, to see it produce walnuts.

Mr Dan's C1 results came out on Thursday, 28 January, at nine in the morning. This time Mr Dan didn't wait for anyone. He got up at six, showered, shaved, put on his Sunday shirt, although it was Thursday, and sat in front of the computer at five to nine, with his wife beside him and his notebook of "pairs" on the table, closed, like a lucky charm. At nine o'clock exactly he pressed the key. He read his name, his candidate number and, in the last column, a single word: APTO. Underneath, the score: sixty-six. His wife screamed. Mr Dan didn't scream. He took off his glasses and covered his face with his hands.

Costel was on the road again, on his second trip, in a rest area near Trieste, when the phone rang. It was Mr Dan. He didn't say hello. He just said: "Sixty-six." It took Costel a second to understand. Then he started shouting in the cab, alone, with the truck stopped, so loudly that a Slovenian trucker parked next to him got out to see if something was wrong. Costel explained to him, in Spanish, that his best friend had just passed the C1. The Slovenian didn't understand a word, but shook his hand and said "congratulations". This time it was Costel who cried, sitting in the cab, with the phone in his hand and the smell of oranges still in the air.

That Saturday, Mr Dan went to the village with his wife, with Ana and with a new frame, identical to the one Costel had given Grandpa in August. Inside was his provisional certificate. Grandpa was waiting for him on the porch, despite the cold, in his Sunday cap. Mr Dan handed him the frame without saying anything. Grandpa looked at it, although he couldn't read it, and then went into the house and hung it on the wall, next to Costel's, at exactly the same height. He stood looking at the two frames for a long time. Then he told Mr Dan, in Romanian, that now he really was at peace, because the wall was complete.

Mr Dan then confessed to him about the lie. He told him he knew he hadn't failed reading the first time, that Costel had told him. Grandpa laughed. He said he knew, that Costel couldn't keep a secret even if you paid him. But he asked him whether the lie had helped. Mr Dan told him yes, a lot, that he had thought about it throughout the exam. Grandpa nodded, satisfied. He told him that, in his experience, lies that were useful stopped being lies as soon as they had done their job. And that this one, therefore, was already true. Mr Dan wrote it down in his notebook, on page two hundred and two.

Before going back to Bucharest, Ana told Grandpa that Ecaterina was leaving for Triana on Monday, 1 February, to write the anthology's introduction in the room upstairs in doña Remedios's bookshop, the one overlooking the orange tree. That she had had her suitcase packed for a week, and that the iron key was hanging on its chain, on the table, next to the tortoiseshell glasses. Grandpa asked how long she would stay. Ana told him a month, or as long as it took. Grandpa thought about it. He said that a woman who went away for a month to write under an orange tree wasn't travelling: she was on her way back.

At seven, Grandpa lit the oil lamp. Ana took out her phone and video-called Costel, who had just arrived in Valencia for the second time and was with Álex in the school garden, making the most of the last light of the afternoon. Álex pointed the phone at the ground. In the soil, next to the stake with the green sign, there was nothing yet. Just dark, wet, freshly watered earth. Grandpa came close to the screen with his glasses on and looked at that patch of earth in silence, very focused, as if he could see through it. Then he said, in Spanish, slowly, a sentence he had learned that very week: "Está dormido. Pero está vivo."

Una foto de 1979 en el mismo banco

Reading text: The child who was wicked
Ecaterina tells the club children about her biggest translation mistake.
When I was young, I translated a novel in which a child was ill, that is, in bed, with a fever.
But I made a mistake and wrote that the child was wicked. So, in Romanian, that poor sick child became a nasty child.
Thirty years later, a reader wrote me a very polite letter. He told me the child didn't seem wicked to him, but sad. He was right. Since then, I'm always careful with ser and estar.
¿Qué le pasaba al niño de la novela?
